               <ns0:p n="7">7 For if the ministration of death <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Deut. 10.1, &c.</ns0:note> written, <ns0:hi>and</ns0:hi> ingraven in stones, was glorious <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">The Apostle is manifestly comparing the Ministry of the Gospel with the Ministry of the Law, and shewing the Excel<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lency of the former above the latter. In the former verse he had called the Law, <ns0:hi>The Letter</ns0:hi>; and the <ns0:hi>Gospel,</ns0:hi> in opposition to it, he had called, <ns0:hi>The Spirit:</ns0:hi> here he calleth the <ns0:hi>Ministra<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tion of the Law, the Ministration of Death</ns0:hi>; because it only shew<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed man his Duty, or things to be done, but give no strength or help, by which he should do them; only cursing man, but shewing him no way by which he might escape that Curse: So it did kill men, and led them to eternal Death and Con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />demnation, without shewing them any means of Life and Sal<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vation. He also undervalueth the Law, in comparison with the Gospel, as being only written, and ingraven upon Stones; whereas (as he had said before,) The Gospel is written in the fleshly Tables of mens hearts. Yet (saith he) the Ministration of the Law (which was indeed but the <ns0:hi>Ministration of Death</ns0:hi>) was glorious: There was a great deal of the Glory and Majesty of God attended the giving of the Law, (of which we read <ns0:hi>Exod.</ns0:hi> 19.)</ns0:note>, so that the children of Israel could not stedfastly behold the face of Moses, for the glory of his countenance, which <ns0:hi>glory</ns0:hi> was to be done away <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>So that the Children of Israel could not stedfastly behold Moses for the glory of his countenance:</ns0:hi> Of this we read <ns0:hi>Exod.</ns0:hi> 34.29, 30. <ns0:hi>When Aaron and all the Children of Israel saw Moses, be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />hold the skin of his face shone, and they were afraid to come nigh him.</ns0:hi> So as it was glorious to be but a Minister of the Law, <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>hat is, of the Revelation of the Will of God, as to <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>ans Duty, <ns0:hi>Which glory</ns0:hi> (saith the Apostle) <ns0:hi>was to be done away; Moses</ns0:hi> his face did not always so shine, neither was the glory of his Mi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nistration to abide always, but to cease by the coming in of the New Covenant.</ns0:note>;</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="8">8 How shall not the ministration of the Spirit be rather glorious? <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">How shall not that Ministration, which is more spiritual, and the effects of which are much more spiritual, be account<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed much more glorious? Thus the Apostle doth not only mag<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nifie the Gospel above the Law, but he also magnifieth his Offices in the <ns0:hi>Ministration of the Gospel</ns0:hi>; which Ministration he reasonably concludeth to be a more glorious Ministration than that which <ns0:hi>Moses</ns0:hi> had, in whom the Jews so much gloried.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="9">9 For if the ministration of condemnation <ns0:hi>be</ns0:hi> glory, much more doth the ministration <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Rom. 3. 2<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>.</ns0:note> of righ<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />teousness exceed in glory <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">What the Apostle before called the <ns0:hi>Ministration of Death,</ns0:hi> he here calleth <ns0:hi>the Ministration of Condemnation</ns0:hi>; and therein gives us a reason, why he called it the Ministration of Death, because it led unto Eternal Death, as shewing men sin, so ac<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cusing and condemning men for sinful acts. If it pleased God (saith the Apostle) to make that Ministration glorious, that the Minister of the Law (<ns0:hi>Moses</ns0:hi>) appeared so glorious in the eyes of <ns0:hi>Aaron,</ns0:hi> and of the People; <ns0:hi>the Ministration of Righte<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ousness</ns0:hi> (by which he means the Gospel) must needs be more exceedingly glorious. He tells us, <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 1.16, 17. <ns0:hi>That he was not ashamed of the Gospel—For therein the Righteousness of God is revealed from faith to faith</ns0:hi>; that is, the Righteousness where<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />in a Soul must stand and appear <ns0:hi>righteous</ns0:hi> before God. The <ns0:hi>Ministration of Righteousness</ns0:hi> signifieth the Ministration of that Gospel, that Doctrine which revealeth <ns0:hi>Righteousness.</ns0:hi> Righte<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ousness is here opposed to <ns0:hi>Condemnation</ns0:hi>; and therefore signifi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />eth that which is opposed to it, <ns0:hi>viz. Iustification.</ns0:hi> For God doth not so freely remit sin, but that he declares his <ns0:hi>Righteous<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ness</ns0:hi> in the remission of them; and will shew himself just, whiles he sheweth himself the <ns0:hi>Iustifier of him that believeth in Iesus, Rom.</ns0:hi> 3.26. And from hence it appeareth, That the Gospel is called the <ns0:hi>Ministration of Righteousness,</ns0:hi> because he that ministreth in it, exhibiteth the Righteousness to Christ to be reckoned to the Soul, as that whereby it must be justified; for God could not otherwise declare his Righteousness in the remission of sins, nor shew himself just in justifying the un<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />godly. This Ministration (he saith) must needs be more glo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rious in the eyes of men, than the Ministration of the Law; for that Ministration afforded nothing but terrour and death, this affordeth relief, and comfort, and life.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="10">10 For even that which was made glorious, had no glory in this respect, by reason of the glory that excelleth <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">The Law had in it something of intrinsick Glory and Ex<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cellency, as it was the Revelation of the Will of God to, and concerning, his Creatures; there was an inseparable Glory at<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tending it upon that account: And it was made glorious in the Ministration of it; as it pleased God that the giving of it should be attended with Thunder and Lightning, Fire and Smoak, and an Earthquake, and a Voice like to the Sound of a Trumpet, (as we read <ns0:hi>Exod.</ns0:hi> 19.16, 17, 18.) this was an acci<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dental and adventitious Glory, and made that which was glo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rious in it self, glorious also in the eyes of the People, that saw and heard these things. But yet (saith the Apostle) if we compare it with the glory of the Gospel, it had compara<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tively no glory; so much doth that excel. For though the Law was the Revelation of the Divine Will, as well as the Go<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />spel, yet the Law was the Revelation of the Divine Will, but as to <ns0:hi>Duty</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Wrath,</ns0:hi> in case of the non-performance of that Duty: but the Gospel is the Revelation of the Divine Will, as to <ns0:hi>Grace</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Mercy,</ns0:hi> as to <ns0:hi>Remission of Sin,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Eternal Life.</ns0:hi> And al<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />though the Gospel came not into the World as the Law, with Thunder, and Lightning, and Earthquakes; yet that was usher<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed in by <ns0:hi>Angels,</ns0:hi> foretelling the Birth and Office of <ns0:hi>Iohn the Baptist,</ns0:hi> and of <ns0:hi>Christ</ns0:hi>; by the great Sign of a Virgins concei<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ving and bringing forth a Son; by a Voice from Heaven, pro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />claiming Christ the Fathers <ns0:hi>only begotten Son, in whom he was well pleased.</ns0:hi> But that which the Apostle doth here principal<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ly intend, is the exceeding Excellency of it, in regard of its further Usefulness and comfortable Nature.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="11">11 For if that which <ns0:hi>was</ns0:hi> done away, <ns0:hi>was</ns0:hi> glorious much more that which remaineth <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> glorious <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">The Apostle, by another Argument, proveth the <ns0:hi>Mini<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stration of the Gospel</ns0:hi> to be much more glorious than the <ns0:hi>Mini<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stration of the Law,</ns0:hi> because it is more <ns0:hi>durable</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>abiding.</ns0:hi> The strength of the Argument dependeth upon this Principle, <ns0:hi>That any durable good is more excellent and glorious, than that which is but transitory, and for a time.</ns0:hi> The Ministration of the Law is done away; the Law, contained in Ordinances, is it self done away; and therefore the Ministration of it must needs cease. There are now no <ns0:hi>Priests</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Levites,</ns0:hi> no <ns0:hi>worldly Sanctuary,</ns0:hi> nor any <ns0:hi>Ministrations</ns0:hi> in it, or relating to it. But our Saviour hath told us, That the <ns0:hi>Gospel</ns0:hi> shall be preached to the End of the World; so as that Ministration must (according to all Principles of Reason) be more glorious, as that which is eternal is more glorious than that which is fluid and vanishing.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="12">
                  <ns0:pb facs="tcp:64193:462" />12 Seeing then that we have such hope, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">
                     <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 word">
                        <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> 6.19.</ns0:note> we use great <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">
                     <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 paragraph">
                        <ns0:desc>〈1 paragraph〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>
                  </ns0:note> plainness of speech <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>Hope</ns0:hi> here signifieth nothing but a confident, certain ex<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pectation of something that is hereafter to come to pass. The term [<ns0:hi>such</ns0:hi>] referreth to something which went before; the sense is, We being in a certain confident expectation, that our Mini<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stration of the Gospel shall not cease, as the Ministration of the Law hath done; and that the Doctrine of the Gospel brings in not a temporary, but an everlasting <ns0:hi>Righteousness</ns0:hi>; that there shall never be any Righteousness revealed, wherein any Soul can stand righteous before God, but that which is revealed in the Gospel to be <ns0:hi>from faith to faith</ns0:hi>; we are neither ashamed, nor afraid to preach the Gospel with all freedom and boldness. We do not, as <ns0:hi>Moses,</ns0:hi> cover our selves with a Veil when we preach the Gospel to people, but we speak what God hath gi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ven to us in Commission to speak, unconcernedly as to any ter<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rours or affrightments from men: we know, that great is the Truth which we preach; and that it shall prevail and out-live all the rage and madness of the Enemies of it.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="13">13 And not as Moses, <ns0:hi>which</ns0:hi> put a veil over his face, that the children of Israel could not stedfast<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ly look <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">
                     <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 word">
                        <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> 10.4.</ns0:note> to the end of that which is abolished <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">We have the History, to which this passage of the Apostle relateth, in <ns0:hi>Exod.</ns0:hi> 34.33.35. where we read, that <ns0:hi>when Moses had done speaking, he put a veil on his face.</ns0:hi> The Apostle here elegantly turns that passage into an <ns0:hi>Allegory,</ns0:hi> and opens to us a <ns0:hi>Mystery</ns0:hi> hidden under that piece of History. That shining of <ns0:hi>Moses</ns0:hi> his Face, in a Type, prefigured the shining of him who was to be <ns0:hi>the Light of the World</ns0:hi>; as he was from Eternity <ns0:hi>the brightness of his Fathers Glory. Moses</ns0:hi> covering himself with a Veil, signifies Gods hiding the Mystery of Christ from Ages. <ns0:hi>Moses</ns0:hi> did not put a Veil on his Face for that end, that the Children of <ns0:hi>Israel</ns0:hi> might not look upon him; but this was the Event of it, which also prefigured the <ns0:hi>blinding</ns0:hi> of the Jews; they first shut their eyes, and would not see, then God judici<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ally sealed their eyes, that they should not see, that Christ was <ns0:hi>the End of the Law for Righteousness,</ns0:hi> the true <ns0:hi>Messiah,</ns0:hi> and the Mediator betwixt God and Man; they could not (as the Apo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stle expresseth it) <ns0:hi>see to the End of that which was to be abolish<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed</ns0:hi>; to the End of the Legal Dispensation, to the End of all the Types of Christ which were in the <ns0:hi>Levitical Law.</ns0:hi> Now (saith the Apostle) we do not do so, but make it our business to preach the Gospel with as much openness, and plainness, and freedom, as is imaginable. The whole History of the Gospel justifieth what this Text affirmeth concerning the Jews; that they could not see, that Christ, by his coming, had put an end to the Law, and the Righteousness thereof. We find upon all occassions how much the <ns0:hi>Pharisees,</ns0:hi> and those who adhered to that Sect, stuck in the Law, to the hindrance of their recei<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ving of, or believing in the Lord Jesus Christ.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="14">14 But <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">
                     <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 span">
                        <ns0:desc>〈…〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>. 10.</ns0:note> their minds were blinded <ns0:note place="bottom">Here the Apostle expoundeth what he meant before by the <ns0:hi>mystical Veil, viz.</ns0:hi> the blinding of the Eyes of the Jews; of which we read often in the New Testament, <ns0:hi>Matt.</ns0:hi> 13.14. <ns0:hi>Mark</ns0:hi> 4.12. <ns0:hi>Luke</ns0:hi> 8.10. <ns0:hi>Ioh.</ns0:hi> 12.40. <ns0:hi>Acts</ns0:hi> 28.26. <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 11.8. (See the Notes upon all those Texts.)</ns0:note>: For until this day remaineth the same veil untaken away <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">And (saith the Apostle) to this day the Veil remaineth not taken away; that Veil, which was signified by the <ns0:hi>Veil</ns0:hi> with which <ns0:hi>Moses</ns0:hi> covered his Face.</ns0:note>, in the reading of the old Testament <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>In the reading of the Old Testament,</ns0:hi> is, when the Old Testa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ment is read: some part of which was wont to be read in the Synagogues every Sabbath-day. But we shall meet with this in the next Verse more fully.</ns0:note>: which <ns0:hi>veil</ns0:hi> is done away in Christ <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">But (saith he) this <ns0:hi>Veil is ta<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ken away in Christ.</ns0:hi> It is really taken away upon the coming of Christ; that is, the <ns0:hi>Veil,</ns0:hi> that covered the Face of Christ, is now truly taken away upon his coming; the Types are fulfilled in him, as their Complement and <ns0:hi>Antitype</ns0:hi>; the Prophecies are fulfilled in him, as he whom they concerned, and of whom the Prophets spake. But the Veil, that is drawn over mens hearts, is not taken away, till they come to receive Jesus Christ, as the End of the Law for Righteousness, to close with him, and to believe in him. God hath taken the Veil off from Christ, by sending him personally to fulfil all Righteousness; but Christ profiteth nothing particular Souls, until they come to believe in him, then it is taken away from their Souls, and not before. Which was the reason, that it remained still upon the Jews, a<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mongst whom he came, as among his own, but they received him not.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="15">15 But even unto this day, when Moses is read, the veil is upon their heart <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">The Veil, mystically signified, by the Veil upon <ns0:hi>Moses</ns0:hi> his face, which hindereth them from seeing, or discerning the Messiah to be come. But why doth he say, <ns0:hi>When Moses,</ns0:hi> that is, the Books of <ns0:hi>Moses,</ns0:hi> or rather of the Old Testament, are read? Possibly he thereby hinteth, that it was their duty, when in the Synagogues they heard the Chapters of the Old Testa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ment read, which contain the Types and Prophecies of Christ, they ought to have looked through those Veils, and have con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sidered Christ as the End of those things; so the Law, as a Schoolmaster, should have led them to Christ: but it was quite otherwise. When they heard those portions of the Old Testa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ment read, through the <ns0:hi>Veil upon their hearts,</ns0:hi> they could not see through the Veil of those Types, Prophecies, and ritual Performances, but rested in them as things, In the performance of which they laid their Righteousness. Or, if they before had some little convictions upon their spirits, yet when they again came into the Synagogues, and heard the Law read, the Veil again appeared over their hearts, so as they could not see Christ.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="16">16 Nevertheless, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Rom. 11.23, 26.</ns0:note> when it shall turn unto the Lord, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Isa. 25.7.</ns0:note> the vail shall be taken away <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>When it shall turn,</ns0:hi> may be understood of the whole, or of the generality (at least) of the Jews, when they shall be con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />verted to the Faith of Christ; Or when any particular person shall be converted to Christ: Then the <ns0:hi>Veil shall be taken away,</ns0:hi> not the Veil with which God covered and veiled the Mysteries of the Gospel (that was already taken away upon Christs co<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ming in the flesh) but the <ns0:hi>Veil</ns0:hi> of blindness, which they had drawn over their own Souls. Though the light of the Gospel shineth clearly, and Christ be unveiled, yet until men, by a true Faith, receive Christ, and turn from sinful courses to the obedience of the Gospel, they see little or nothing of Christ. The <ns0:hi>taking away of this Veil,</ns0:hi> and the <ns0:hi>turning to the Lord,</ns0:hi> are things done in Souls at the same time; therefore nothing is to be concluded here, from the Apostles naming the removal of the impediment, after the effect of which that is a cause.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="17">17 Now the Lord is that Spirit <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">The Lord Christ was a <ns0:hi>Man,</ns0:hi> but not a <ns0:hi>meer Man</ns0:hi>; but one who had the Divine Nature personally united to his humane Nature, which is called the <ns0:hi>Spirit, Mark</ns0:hi> 2.8. But some think, that the Article here, is not meerly <ns0:hi>Prepositive,</ns0:hi> but <ns0:hi>Emphati<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cal</ns0:hi>; and so referreth to <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 6. where the Gospel (the substance of which is Christ) was called <ns0:hi>the Spirit.</ns0:hi> So it is judged by some, that the Apostle preventeth a Question which some might have propounded, <ns0:hi>viz.</ns0:hi> how the <ns0:hi>Veil</ns0:hi> should be taken away by mens turning unto the Lord? Saith the Apostle, The Lord is a Spirit, or he is that Spirit mentioned <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 18. he is a Spirit, and he gives out of the Spirit unto his People, the Spirit of Holi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ness and Sanctification.</ns0:note>, and where the Spirit of the Lord <ns0:hi>is,</ns0:hi> there <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> liberty <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">And where the Spirit of the Lord is, (that holy sanctifying Spirit, which is often called the Spi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rit of Christ) there is <ns0:hi>liberty</ns0:hi>; (for our Saviour told the Jews, <ns0:hi>Ioh.</ns0:hi> 8.36. <ns0:hi>If the Son make you free, then shall you be free indeed</ns0:hi>) A liberty from the yoke of the Law, from Sin, Death, Hell; but the liberty which seemeth here to be chiefly intended, is a <ns0:hi>liberty</ns0:hi> from that <ns0:hi>blindness</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>hardness</ns0:hi> which is upon mens hearts, until they have received the holy Spirit.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="18">18 But we all with open face beholding <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">1 Cor. 13.12.</ns0:note> as in a glass <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 4.4, 6. 1 Tim. 1.11.</ns0:note> the glory of the Lord <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">Some by [<ns0:hi>we</ns0:hi>] here understand all Believers; others think it is better understood of Ministers: but the universal Particle <ns0:hi>all,</ns0:hi> rather guideth us to interpret it of the whole body of Believers, of whom the Apostle saith, That they all behold the glory of God <ns0:hi>with open face,</ns0:hi> that is, not under those dark Types, Shadows, and Prophecies, that he was of old revealed under, but as in a Looking-glass, which represents the face as at hand; not as in a Perspective, which sheweth things afar off.</ns0:note>, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">1 Cor. 15.49. Col. 3.10.</ns0:note> are changed into the same image from glory to glory <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">We behold him in the glass of the Gospel, fully open<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed and preached; and this sight of Christ in the Gospel, is not a meer useless sight, but such a sight as changeth the Soul into the image and likeness of Christ, from <ns0:hi>glory</ns0:hi> to <ns0:hi>glory</ns0:hi>; car<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rying on the Souls of Believers from one degree of Grace to another; or making such a glorious change in the heart, as shall not be blotted out until a Soul cometh into those possessi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ons of Glory which God hath prepared for his People.</ns0:note>, even as <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>of the Lord the Spirit.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> by the Spirit of the Lord <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">And all this is done by the Spirit of the Lord, working with the Word of God in the mouths of his Ministers; but so, as the Spirit hath the principal agency and efficiency in the work.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
